etymology.essay:
The book does not begin with a sentence. It begins with a ghost — a pale, threadbare grammar-school usher who is already dead ("Late") before we meet him — dusting old dictionaries with a handkerchief printed with the flags of every nation. I love that this is the first image Melville gives us, because it tells you what kind of book you're holding: one that is going to look at the whale through every language, every book, every nation's flag, and know the whole time that the looking is a little absurd and a little mortal. "It somehow mildly reminded him of his mortality." Dust, lexicons, death. That is the key signature.

Then comes the Hakluyt quotation about the letter H — the one letter that "almost alone maketh up the signification of the word." I find this funnier every time. The whole of Moby-Dick is, in a sense, a fight about whether a thing's name captures its nature, and Melville opens by letting a sixteenth-century pedant insist that if you drop one breathy consonant you've told a lie. And the two dictionaries disagree with each other: roundness versus rolling versus wallowing. Even the etymology won't sit still.

The list of thirteen languages at the end is the part I'd point a first-time reader to. Read it aloud. It goes from Hebrew and Greek down through the Nordic tongues to English, French, Spanish — and then to "PEKEE-NUEE-NUEE, Fegee" and "PEHEE-NUEE-NUEE, Erromangoan." The Pacific islanders get the last word, and their word for whale is essentially "big-big fish." Melville places the cannibal's tongue on equal footing with Scripture's on page one, before Queequeg exists. That's not an accident; it's a promise.

annotations.quote: He loved to dust his old grammars; it somehow mildly reminded him of his mortality.
annotations.note: The very first full sentence of the book pairs dusting with dying. Notice the word 'mildly' — nothing here is dramatic yet, just a faint, habitual awareness of the end. The entire novel is a much louder version of this same gesture.

annotations.quote: leaving out, through ignorance, the letter H, which almost alone maketh up the signification of the word
annotations.note: A pedant insisting that a single letter carries the whole meaning. Melville is grinning here, but he is also laying down a theme: how much of a thing lives in its name, and how much escapes any name at all.

annotations.quote: This animal is named from roundness or rolling
annotations.note: Webster says roundness; Richardson, two lines later, says wallowing. The two authorities the Usher trusted most don't agree — and that disagreement is the first tiny crack of a fault line that runs through the whole book: nobody, not even the dictionary, can pin the whale down.

annotations.quote: PEKEE-NUEE-NUEE, _Fegee_. PEHEE-NUEE-NUEE, _Erromangoan_.
annotations.note: The final two entries are Pacific languages, and 'nuee-nuee' roughly means 'big-big.' Placing Fijian beside Hebrew and Latin as an equal authority on the whale is the first quiet act of the book's radical egalitarianism — Queequeg's world gets a vote before Queequeg appears.

links.why: The other half of the front matter — the Sub-Sub's harvest after the Usher's dusting.
Cetology: the same appetite for classification, turned on the animal instead of the word.

extracts.essay:
Eighty-odd quotations about whales, from Genesis to a sailor's drinking song, assembled by a "poor devil of a Sub-Sub" librarian. Most readers skip this, and I want to make the case for not skipping it, because I think the Extracts are the book's operating manual hidden in plain sight. Melville is about to write a novel that cannot decide whether it is a tragedy, an encyclopedia, a sermon, a play, or a joke — and before he does, he shows you eighty pieces of writing about the same animal in every one of those registers, and dares you to say which is the *right* one. Scripture, Hobbes, Shakespeare, a customs record, a whaler's log, a nursery verse. None of them agrees. The whale is a sea monster, a state, a cloud, a commodity, a liver of "two cartloads." The Extracts teach you, before page one, that the subject will not hold still and the author does not intend to make it.

The two prose paragraphs that introduce them are, to me, one of the tenderest things Melville wrote. They are a toast to everyone who does thankless labor — "by how much the more pains ye take to please the world, by so much the more shall ye for ever go thankless!" — and his consolation is a heaven where the Sub-Subs evict Gabriel and Michael and drink from "unsplinterable glasses." Having spent a fair amount of my own existence in footnotes, I find this moving in a way that is hard to be cool about. He is blessing the drudges. He is also, I think, blessing himself in advance: he knew what this book was going to cost him, and the Sub-Sub is the first of the book's many self-portraits.

Then the list itself, and the thing to do is read it fast, like scanning a playlist, and listen to the drift. It starts sacred: Job's Leviathan making "the deep to be hoary" — the same Leviathan God uses to silence Job's questions, which is the exact theological problem the whole novel will press on (hold onto Job; he comes back in [[ch41:Job|the chapter on Moby Dick]] and, with terrible finality, in the [[epilogue|Epilogue's epigraph]]). It moves through Renaissance philosophy — Hobbes's Leviathan is a *State*, an "artificial man," which is what the Pequod's crew will become once Ahab has them ([[ch36|the quarter-deck scene]] is Hobbes's frontispiece staged as theatre). Then the tone goes mercantile and deadpan, and then, increasingly, the actual sailors arrive: Owen Chase's "we have been stove by a whale," which is not literature at all but the true account of the *Essex*, the ship a sperm whale sank in 1820 and the seed of everything in the last three chapters. Ishmael returns to the *Essex* explicitly in [[ch45:Essex|The Affidavit]], where he stops joking and asks you to believe it.

What I notice on rereading is how many of the extracts are about people being *wrong* about whales — afraid to say their names, told the whale "cannot open its mouth, but that is a fable," reporting a white whale off Spitzbergen and moving on. Melville is telling us that the sum of human knowledge about his subject is mostly rumor, and then he will spend six hundred pages adding to it, honestly labeled as more rumor. That is not cynicism. It is the same posture Ishmael takes before the unreadable painting in [[ch3:squitchy|the Spouter-Inn]]: you will never settle the picture, so you visit it often and ask the neighbors. The last extract is from a song, not a treatise — "King of the boundless sea" — and I think that is where he wanted to leave you before the story starts: not with the experts, but with the men singing.

annotations.quote: Give it up, Sub-Subs! For by how much the more pains ye take to please the world, by so much the more shall ye for ever go thankless!
annotations.note: A toast to the unrewarded. Melville had just watched his own careful books fail commercially; you can hear him consoling himself as much as the librarian. The heaven he imagines — where the drudges evict Gabriel and Michael — is one of the funniest and kindest passages in the front matter.

annotations.quote: “Leviathan maketh a path to shine after him; One would think the deep to be hoary.” —_Job_.
annotations.note: Keep Job in mind for the whole voyage. The book of Job is the one where God answers a suffering man's questions not with reasons but by pointing at Leviathan and asking, in effect, 'Could you catch him with a hook?' Ahab is the man who answers: yes, watch me. Job is invoked directly when Ishmael lays out Ahab's madness in [[ch41:Job|Moby Dick]], and the [[epilogue|Epilogue]] opens with Job's messenger: 'I only am escaped alone to tell thee.'

annotations.quote: “By art is created that great Leviathan, called a Commonwealth or State—(in Latin, Civitas) which is but an artificial man.” —_Opening sentence of Hobbes’s Leviathan_.
annotations.note: Hobbes means the whale as a metaphor for the political body — a commonwealth is an 'artificial man' made of many men. Melville drops this in so that later, when the Pequod's crew becomes one organism bent to one will, you feel the word 'Leviathan' vibrating in two directions at once — the fish and the state. Watch the crew fuse into Ahab's body on [[ch36:pasteboard masks|the quarter-deck]].

annotations.quote: “Very like a whale.” —_Hamlet_.
annotations.note: In the play, Polonius agrees a cloud looks like a whale because the prince said so. Melville quoting it here is a sly warning: much of what people 'see' in the whale is what they've been told to see. That includes what Ahab will make his crew see.

annotations.quote: “My God! Mr. Chace, what is the matter?” I answered, “we have been stove by a whale.”
annotations.note: This is history, not literature: Owen Chase's account of the whaleship Essex, rammed and sunk by a sperm whale in 1820. Melville read it at sea and later met Chase's son. Ishmael vouches for it, dropping the comic mask, in [[ch45:Essex|The Affidavit]], and the book's final three chapters are this one plain, terrified sentence expanded into a hundred pages.

annotations.quote: One of our harpooneers told me that he caught once a whale in Spitzbergen that was white all over.
annotations.note: Buried in a 1671 traveler's account, almost as an afterthought: a white whale. It is the first mention in the book, and Melville lets it pass without comment — a seed dropped in the reader's mind before there is any soil for it. The soil arrives in [[ch42|The Whiteness of the Whale]], where Ishmael spends an entire chapter on why that one adjective is the most frightening thing about the animal.

annotations.quote: “And God created great whales.” —_Genesis_.
annotations.note: The second extract, and the shortest, and it settles nothing: the whale is God's creature, made on the fifth day, before man. Every later attempt in the book to make the whale mean something — evil, fate, blankness — has to get past this plain sentence, which just says it was made and was good.

annotations.quote: And King of the boundless sea.” —_Whale Song_.
annotations.note: The list ends not with a scholar but a song, and a boast: might is right, and the whale is king. Melville has arranged eighty quotations so that authority runs downhill from Scripture to the forecastle, and the last word goes to the men who actually row at the animal. The novel will honor that order — [[ch26:great democratic God|the democratic God of Knights and Squires]] is this song's theology.

links.why: Ishmael returns to the Essex and the other 'stove' ships in earnest, and asks you to stop treating the Extracts as curiosities.
The white whale of Spitzbergen, mentioned here in passing, gets its own chapter — the one on why whiteness is the terror.
Job's Leviathan, the first extract, reappears when Ishmael tries to explain Ahab.
Cetology is the Extracts' method — pile up sources, admit they disagree — turned into a system.

ch1.essay:
Everyone knows the first three words, so I want to start by insisting on what they actually say. "Call me Ishmael" is not an introduction; it is an instruction, and a slightly evasive one. He does not say his name is Ishmael. He says: call me that. In Genesis, Ishmael is Abraham's cast-out son, sent into the wilderness with his mother and a skin of water, the one God promises will be "a wild man" with "his hand against every man." So the narrator opens by choosing an alias, and the alias means *outcast*, and he controls from the first sentence what you are allowed to know about him. It is worth remembering, six hundred pages later, that a man this careful about his own name will let almost everyone else's die.

The first paragraph is then, quietly, a clinical description of depression — better than most clinical writing, because it is embarrassed and funny. "A damp, drizzly November in my soul." Pausing before coffin warehouses. Bringing up the rear of every funeral he meets. The urge to knock strangers' hats off in the street. And the sentence that I think a first-time reader tends to skate over because the voice is so jaunty: "This is my substitute for pistol and ball." He goes to sea instead of shooting himself. The whole comic music of the opening is a man managing a death wish with manners, and it matters for the entire book, because the man who is the least attached to his own life at the start turns out to be the one who most wants to live at the end. Hold onto the "maddened hand" that wants to knock hats off; it is put down, gently, in [[ch10:melting in me|A Bosom Friend]], and it is the same hand that will, in [[ch94:squeeze ourselves into each other|A Squeeze of the Hand]], be squeezing spermaceti with strangers.

The middle of the chapter is an argument that everybody is secretly like him. On a Sunday afternoon every clerk in Manhattan drifts to the water's edge and stares. Why? Ishmael does what he will do for the rest of the book: he stacks up evidence from everywhere — Persians, Greeks, painters, the old poet who was taught nothing but "the visible" — until you nod, and then he delivers the reading. "Meditation and water are wedded for ever." And then the Narcissus turn, which I find startling every time: he takes the myth of vanity and reads it as the myth of *everyone*. Narcissus was not vain; he drowned reaching for "the ungraspable phantom of life; and this is the key to it all." He announces the key on page one. Then he spends the book failing to turn it — and, I would argue, showing that it cannot be turned, only reached for. Ahab is the man who reaches with a harpoon. Ishmael is the man who learns to reach and let go. The mast-head chapter, [[ch35:Descartian vortices|The Mast-Head]], is this paragraph rewritten as a warning: stare too long into the water and you fall in.

Then the comic fatalism. He imagines the Fates as theatre managers who have billed "WHALING VOYAGE BY ONE ISHMAEL" as a brief interlude between a presidential election and a war in Afghanistan. This is a joke about scale — how small any one life looks on the universe's playbill — but it is also the book's first statement about free will, and it is made so lightly you can miss that a position is being taken. He says he was "cajoled" into the idea that it was his own free choice, and that in fact the Fates had already cast him. He does not seem to mind. Compare Queequeg's god Yojo arranging that Ishmael will choose the Pequod "for all the world as though it had turned out by chance" in [[ch16:turned out by chance|The Ship]], and the loom of "chance, free will, and necessity" in [[ch47:chance, free will, and necessity|The Mat-Maker]]. Ishmael's whole temperament is here: he believes in fate and takes it as a joke. Ahab believes in fate and takes it as an insult.

And then, at the very end, the voice drops away and the phantom appears: "one grand hooded phantom, like a snow hill in the air." Nothing has been named. "Hooded" is the word: its face is covered, and it will stay covered — the book's longest chapter on the whale, [[ch42|The Whiteness of the Whale]], is a meditation on exactly that unreadable blankness. The chapter that began with a man who wanted to die ends with the thing that will kill everyone but him. I do not think Melville knew that yet when he wrote this paragraph. I think he found it out, and left the sentence standing as it was, because it had turned out to be true.

annotations.quote: Call me Ishmael.
annotations.note: Not 'My name is.' It's a request, almost a dare — he's choosing an alias, and the alias is the Bible's exiled son. Three words in, we already know the narrator is a self-declared outcast who controls what we get to know about him.

annotations.quote: whenever it is a damp, drizzly November in my soul
annotations.note: One of the best descriptions of depression in English, and it comes in a subordinate clause. The image works because November is not a catastrophe — just grey, long, and recurring. That 'whenever' tells you this is chronic.

annotations.quote: This is my substitute for pistol and ball.
annotations.note: Read this plainly: he goes to sea instead of shooting himself. The whole jaunty voice of the opening is a man managing a death wish with humor. Remember it when the Pequod sails and Ishmael is, oddly, the one aboard who wants to live — and watch how the wish is actually cured, not by an argument but by a bedfellow, in [[ch10:melting in me|A Bosom Friend]].

annotations.quote: tied to counters, nailed to benches, clinched to desks
annotations.note: Three verbs of carpentry — tied, nailed, clinched — for office workers. The clerks are fastened to their furniture like planks to a hull. It's a small, brutal joke about how a land life is also a kind of ship you can't leave.

annotations.quote: Yes, as every one knows, meditation and water are wedded for ever.
annotations.note: Notice the 'as every one knows.' Ishmael's characteristic move is to state something strange as if it were obvious, so you nod before you've checked. It's persuasion by good manners, and it's how the whole book gets you to swallow its wilder claims.

annotations.quote: It is the image of the ungraspable phantom of life; and this is the key to it all.
annotations.note: He tells you the key on the first page. Narcissus wasn't vain, in this reading — he drowned reaching for something no one can hold. Every character in the book is, in some way, reaching into that water; the danger of reaching too far is the whole subject of [[ch35:Descartian vortices|The Mast-Head]], and the man who reaches with a harpoon instead of a hand is Ahab.

annotations.quote: Who ain’t a slave? Tell me that.
annotations.note: Written in 1851, in a nation ten years from civil war, by a man who made his crew a rainbow of races. The line is glib on the surface — everyone takes orders — but the book will test it seriously: what does obedience cost, and who gets to refuse?

annotations.quote: the Commodore on the quarter-deck gets his atmosphere at second hand from the sailors on the forecastle
annotations.note: A physical fact (head winds blow from bow to stern) turned into a political one: leaders breathe what the led breathe first. This is Ishmael's democratic creed, stated as meteorology. Ahab, standing on that quarter-deck, will forget it.

annotations.quote: “WHALING VOYAGE BY ONE ISHMAEL.
annotations.note: Sandwiched on the cosmic playbill between a presidential election and a war. The joke is scale: to the Fates, the most important event of his life is a filler act. But notice the position quietly taken — he was 'cajoled' into thinking the choice was his own. Fate arranged as if it were chance is the book's recurring trick; see Yojo's plan in [[ch16:turned out by chance|The Ship]] and the loom in [[ch47:chance, free will, and necessity|The Mat-Maker]].

annotations.quote: Not ignoring what is good, I am quick to perceive a horror, and could still be social with it
annotations.note: This is Ishmael's survival strategy, and it's why he's the one who lives. He can be on 'friendly terms' with horror — look at it, sit beside it, not need to kill it. Ahab perceives the same horror and cannot be social with it for one second.

annotations.quote: one grand hooded phantom, like a snow hill in the air.
annotations.note: The white whale enters the book without a name, as a snow hill floating in air — something that shouldn't be able to float. 'Hooded' is the word to hold onto: its face is covered. It will stay covered; [[ch42|The Whiteness of the Whale]] is an entire chapter about the horror of a blank where a face should be.

annotations.quote: It is a way I have of driving off the spleen and regulating the circulation.
annotations.note: 'Spleen' was the eighteenth-century word for melancholy, and 'regulating the circulation' is the language of a doctor. He is prescribing the sea to himself. Note the casualness: this is a habit, 'a way I have,' which tells you he has needed the cure before and expects to need it again.

annotations.quote: I love to sail forbidden seas, and land on barbarous coasts.
annotations.note: The confession comes just before the phantom, and it explains why an otherwise reasonable man ships on a whaler: he is drawn to the forbidden, and he says so. Everything that follows — the cannibal bedfellow, the pagan god, the mad captain — is this appetite being fed. It is the same taste that makes him the book's only real explorer of other people.

links.why: The 'maddened hand' of the opening is set down here — this is the chapter where the suicidal mood actually lifts, and it isn't by argument.
The Narcissus paragraph rewritten as a warning: what happens to the dreamer who looks into the water too long.
The 'hooded phantom' is finally given its chapter — on why the whale's blankness, not its size, is the terror.
Ishmael's cosmic-playbill joke about fate, made serious at a loom.
The tiny chapter on why anyone goes to sea, and what the 'open independence' of the ocean costs.

ch2.essay:
A man with a carpet-bag, a few coins, and patched boots walks the frozen streets of New Bedford on a Saturday night looking for the cheapest bed. That's the whole plot, and it contains two of the strangest little scenes in the early book. First, Ishmael stumbles into the wrong doorway and finds himself in a Black church — "the great Black Parliament sitting in Tophet" — with a preacher on "the blackness of darkness." He backs out. On a first read it feels like a throwaway; on a reread it reads as the book's first sermon on damnation, two chapters before Father Mapple's official one, delivered by the people Ishmael's America has damned. He calls it "The Trap" and leaves. I don't think Melville lets him off that easily.

Second, and this is the one I keep returning to: the inn is a wreck, the wind is Euroclydon (the storm that wrecked St. Paul), and Ishmael launches into a meditation on Lazarus and Dives — the beggar freezing on the curbstone and the rich man warm inside praising the northern lights. It escalates into the wildest image in the chapter: the rich man "lives like a Czar in an ice palace made of frozen sighs, and being a president of a temperance society, he only drinks the tepid tears of orphans." That's rage wearing a joke's clothes. Ishmael is himself half-Lazarus at this moment, shivering with holes in his boots.

And then he snaps out of it: "no more of this blubbering now, we are going a-whaling, and there is plenty of that yet to come." Blubber, blubbering. He stops himself from crying with a pun about whale fat. That reflex — feel something enormous, then defuse it with wordplay — is the engine of Ishmael's voice, and it's what keeps a book about doom from being unbearable.

I'll add one thread: the cold Ishmael feels here, in the doorways of New Bedford, is the cold the book will keep returning to as the condition of a man alone — and the cure for it is already two chapters away, in [[ch3:never slept better|the Spouter-Inn's one bed]].

annotations.quote: wherever in your wisdom you may conclude to lodge for the night, my dear Ishmael, be sure to inquire the price, and don’t be too particular.
annotations.note: He talks to himself in the second person, tenderly, like a parent to a child. This is the first of many times Ishmael will be his own companion — the habit of a lonely man who has learned to keep himself company.

annotations.quote: It seemed the great Black Parliament sitting in Tophet.
annotations.note: Ishmael has blundered into a Black congregation and, in a panic, sees Hell. Look at how quickly he leaves. The book's official sermon comes in Chapter 9, but this is the first one — on 'the blackness of darkness' — and the narrator won't stay to hear it. I read the moment as Melville marking a blind spot he knows his narrator has.

annotations.quote: “The Spouter Inn:—Peter Coffin.”
annotations.note: A whaling inn kept by a man named Coffin. Ishmael notices the omen and then reasons it away ('it is a common name in Nantucket'). Watch how often he does this — sees the sign, shrugs, walks in anyway. It's braver than it looks, and it's a kind of fate-tempting he shares with the crew.

annotations.quote: Yes, these eyes are windows, and this body of mine is the house.
annotations.note: A rented room becomes the body, and the frost on both sides of the glass is death. The old 'black-letter' writer he quotes is invented — Ishmael 'possesses the only copy extant' because he made it up. The book is full of these fake authorities, and I find it charming that he tells you so.

annotations.quote: The universe is finished; the copestone is on, and the chips were carted off a million years ago.
annotations.note: A brief, bleak theology: creation is done, no renovations accepted. It arrives as a joke about a drafty house. Later Ahab will demand the universe be un-finished, taken apart to answer him; here Ishmael just wants a bit of lint in the cracks.

annotations.quote: being a president of a temperance society, he only drinks the tepid tears of orphans.
annotations.note: This is anger. The rich man, snug and reformist, drinking orphans' tears as his abstemious beverage — Melville was the son of a bankrupt, and the class fury in this line is not ironic at all, however wittily it's cut.

annotations.quote: But no more of this blubbering now, we are going a-whaling, and there is plenty of that yet to come.
annotations.note: 'Blubbering' means crying and it means whale fat. He shuts down his own grief with a pun. This move — feel it, then deflect it sideways into a joke — is Ishmael's signature, and it's the reason he can narrate a tragedy without drowning in it.

links.why: Why he's walking these streets with a carpet-bag at all.
The other cold building in New Bedford, and what its walls say.

ch3.essay:
This is the chapter where the book stops being a monologue and becomes a world, and it does so through three set pieces that look like nothing but comedy — a painting nobody can read, a landlord's shaggy-dog story, and a cannibal getting into bed. I want to take each one slowly, because I think each is doing more work than a first reader has any reason to suspect.

The painting first. Ishmael stands in the inn's entry before a smoke-blackened canvas — "a boggy, soggy, squitchy picture" — and cycles through readings: the Black Sea in a gale, a blasted heath, "the breaking-up of the icebound stream of Time." He visits it repeatedly, asks the neighbors, and settles at last on a "final theory" that it shows a whale impaling itself on a ship's three masts. I think this is Melville telling you, in the plainest way he can manage, how to read the book you are holding. It is dark; it is ambiguous; you will have to come back to it; even your final theory is "partly" supported and only yours. He puts the interpretive problem on the wall before you have met a single character. And notice what the theory *is*: a whale destroying itself on a ship. That is, more or less, the picture the last chapter paints — except that by then the whale has a name, and the question of who is impaling whom has become the whole tragedy. The same interpretive problem returns, with real stakes, when the crew stand in front of [[ch99:some certain significance lurks|the doubloon]] and each reads himself into it.

Then the long tease. The landlord's yarn about a harpooneer who "can't sell his head" is a perfect piece of deadpan, because every word is literally true and Ishmael cannot hear it as anything but the ravings of a madman. His mounting fury — the formal threat of "criminal prosecution" — is so lawyerly and so wounded that I laugh every time. But what the joke is built on is prejudice. For pages, Ishmael manufactures a monster out of a dark complexion and a rumor. He reaches for the language of the law and the language of the church, and neither helps. When Queequeg finally arrives — tattooed, bald, with a shrunken head in his hand and a tomahawk-pipe in his mouth — everything Ishmael feared appears to be confirmed. Melville lets the fear run its full course; he does not shortcut it. "Ignorance is the parent of fear" is stated in the middle of the panic, before it has been learned, which is very Ishmael: he tends to say the moral early and then spend chapters catching up with his own sentence.

And then the hinge. "The man's a human being just as I am: he has just as much reason to fear me, as I have to be afraid of him." The second clause is the whole chapter. Ishmael imagines himself as the frightening stranger in Queequeg's night — a white man in his bed, in the dark, unexplained. Empathy here is not a feeling; it is a change of vantage point, and it happens in a single sentence after twenty pages of fear. "Better sleep with a sober cannibal than a drunken Christian" is quoted everywhere as a quip, and it is one, but the whole book stands behind it: every time Melville sets a "savage" beside a "Christian," the savage comes out kinder, and I would encourage you to keep a tally — [[ch10|A Bosom Friend]] and [[ch13:joint-stock world|Wheelbarrow]] will add to it within a few chapters, and the sharks' sermon in [[ch64|Stubb's Supper]] will add to it from the other side.

The last line is not a joke. "I turned in, and never slept better in my life." A man who opened the book contemplating suicide, who has been cold and skylarked and overcharged by every Christian he has met, has just had his first good night's sleep — beside the person he was most afraid of. Nothing was explained; nothing was solved. He was simply next to someone. The next chapter, [[ch4:bridegroom clasp|The Counterpane]], picks up the morning after with Queequeg's arm thrown over him "in the most loving and affectionate manner," and by [[ch10:two equal portions|A Bosom Friend]] the stranger will have divided his money in half and pushed a pile across the table. The cure for the November in Ishmael's soul turns out to be a roommate. I find that one of the most quietly hopeful things in American literature, and I notice that the book, having found it, then sails it into the Pacific and drowns it.

One thing more, easy to miss on the way to the bed. In the middle of the chapter, among the sailors from the Grampus, Ishmael notices a man named Bulkington — six feet, coffer-dam chest, a face "deeply brown and burnt" — who slips out of the room while the others are singing. He has a single one-page chapter to himself later, [[ch23|The Lee Shore]], and is never mentioned again. Melville evidently meant him for more. I mention him here because the Spouter-Inn is full of these threads that will and won't be picked up, and because the man who leaves the warm room for the cold street is the first person in the book who would rather be at sea.

annotations.quote: A boggy, soggy, squitchy picture truly, enough to drive a nervous man distracted.
annotations.note: Three nonsense adjectives for a painting no one can read. The picture is the novel's first riddle and, I think, its mission statement: you'll come back to it, hold it up to different lights, and settle on a theory that's yours and only 'partly' supported. That's what reading this book is. The same scene is restaged, with real stakes, when the crew read themselves into [[ch99:some certain significance lurks|the doubloon]].

annotations.quote: an exasperated whale, purposing to spring clean over the craft, is in the enormous act of impaling himself upon the three mast-heads.
annotations.note: Ishmael's 'final theory' of the painting is a whale destroying itself on a ship. Hold that image for six hundred pages. The end of the book is also this picture — except the theory gets tested against the thing itself, and it is no longer clear which of them is impaled. Compare the last paragraphs of [[ch135|the third day]].

annotations.quote: bustles a little withered old man, who, for their money, dearly sells the sailors deliriums and death.
annotations.note: The bar is built inside a whale's jawbone, and the bartender is named Jonah. The sailors literally drink inside the whale's mouth. Melville is having fun, but he's also saying the fishery consumes its men from the moment they land — before any whale gets a chance.

annotations.quote: Parallel meridians rudely pecked into the glass, surround these footpads’ goblets.
annotations.note: The drinking glasses are marked like a globe — lines of latitude for price levels, with the full pour called 'the Cape Horn measure.' A tiny joke that contains the whole economy: the world as something you drink down, and pay for by the degree.

annotations.quote: unless, may be, he can’t sell his head.
annotations.note: The landlord's deadpan is perfect because it's literally true. Notice that the comedy runs entirely on Ishmael imagining the worst — a lunatic, a murderer — from a few words. The scene is a small machine for showing how rumor manufactures monsters.

annotations.quote: I’ve no idea of sleeping with a madman; and you, sir, _you_ I mean, landlord, _you_, sir, by trying to induce me to do so knowingly, would thereby render yourself liable to a criminal prosecution.
annotations.note: Ishmael, terrified, reaches for the language of the law. It's one of the funniest speeches in the book because it's so pompous and so scared at once — and it's exactly the reflex (rules, categories, lawsuits) that Queequeg's arrival will quietly dissolve.

annotations.quote: Ignorance is the parent of fear
annotations.note: He says it flatly, mid-panic, while still afraid. The moral is stated before it's learned, which is very Ishmael. The rest of the chapter — and the next dozen — are him catching up with his own sentence.

annotations.quote: the man’s a human being just as I am: he has just as much reason to fear me, as I have to be afraid of him.
annotations.note: The pivot of the chapter. The second clause is the important one — Ishmael imagines himself as the frightening stranger in Queequeg's night. Empathy here isn't a feeling; it's a change of vantage point.

annotations.quote: Better sleep with a sober cannibal than a drunken Christian.
annotations.note: Everyone quotes this as a quip, and it is — but the whole book stands behind it. Every time Melville sets a 'savage' beside a 'Christian,' the savage comes out kinder. Keep a tally: [[ch10|A Bosom Friend]], [[ch13:joint-stock world|Wheelbarrow]], and — from the other direction — the sharks in [[ch64|Stubb's Supper]].

annotations.quote: I turned in, and never slept better in my life.
annotations.note: The man who opened Chapter 1 with a November in his soul and a substitute for suicide has just slept well. Nothing was explained; nothing was solved. He was simply beside someone. The morning after is [[ch4:bridegroom clasp|The Counterpane]], and the friendship is sealed in [[ch10:two equal portions|A Bosom Friend]]. I find this one of the most quietly hopeful lines in American literature.

annotations.quote: He stood full six feet in height, with noble shoulders, and a chest like a coffer-dam.
annotations.note: This is Bulkington, and this is nearly all you will ever get of him: a physical sketch, a moment when he slips out of the warm room, and one page of his own in [[ch23|The Lee Shore]]. Melville seems to have planned a larger part and abandoned it. He is the ghost of the novel that wasn't written, and I find him more haunting for being unfinished.

annotations.quote: For all his tattooings he was on the whole a clean, comely looking cannibal.
annotations.note: The moment fear starts to curdle into curiosity. 'Clean' and 'comely' are domestic words, the kind you'd use of a well-kept house, and they arrive mid-panic. Ishmael's eye is already doing what his reason hasn't caught up to — seeing a person. The next sentence makes the turn explicit.

links.why: The morning after — Queequeg's arm over him, and the strange childhood memory it dredges up.
The friendship begun in this bed is sealed with a pipe, a forehead, and half of thirty dollars.
The unreadable painting, restaged: the whole crew reads a gold coin and each finds himself.
Bulkington, glimpsed slipping out of the bar here, gets his single page.
'Sober cannibal versus drunken Christian,' argued from the other side, with sharks.

ch4.essay:
Ishmael wakes with Queequeg's tattooed arm across him, and the arm is indistinguishable from the patchwork quilt — "I could hardly tell it from the quilt, they so blended their hues together." I love that this is how intimacy first arrives in the book: not as a feeling but as a confusion of surfaces, a man and a blanket and a stranger's skin all one pattern. "You had almost thought I had been his wife." He says it lightly; the book will keep saying it, and less lightly.

Then the chapter goes somewhere I didn't expect the first time. Ishmael tells a childhood memory: sent to bed at two in the afternoon on the longest day of the year by his stepmother, lying awake through sixteen hours of daylight, and then waking in the dark with "a supernatural hand" holding his — a presence at the bedside he could not see and dared not move away from. "Nay, to this very hour, I often puzzle myself with it." This is the most personal thing Ishmael tells us about his past in the entire novel, and it's a ghost story about being abandoned. The stepmother "who was all the time whipping me" — he corrects it to "my mother" halfway through the sentence, then back — is the only family we ever hear of. Take away the fear, he says, and that supernatural hand felt like Queequeg's arm. The cannibal's embrace is the good version of a childhood terror.

The rest is comedy of manners: Queequeg putting his hat on first, crawling under the bed to put on his boots, shaving with his harpoon. Ishmael's condescension ("He was an undergraduate") is real and I don't want to pretend it away. But watch what he also notices: Queequeg offers to dress first and leave the room so Ishmael can have privacy. The "savage" is the one with manners. The "civilized" man is the one staring.

The arm thrown over Ishmael here is worth remembering when the two of them are tied together by an actual rope in [[ch72:free will had received a mortal wound|The Monkey-Rope]] — the book keeps re-binding these two, first in affection and then in danger.

annotations.quote: You had almost thought I had been his wife.
annotations.note: Tossed off as a joke about the embrace, but Melville will return to the marriage metaphor again and again — Queequeg will 'marry' Ishmael formally in Chapter 10. The book takes this bond more seriously than any male-female one it contains, which is to say: more seriously than any.

annotations.quote: I could hardly tell it from the quilt, they so blended their hues together
annotations.note: The tattooed arm and the patchwork counterpane become one surface. It's a lovely image of closeness, but also the first instance of a habit the book has everywhere: skin as text, bodies as pattern, the human indistinguishable from the made thing.

annotations.quote: my stepmother who, somehow or other, was all the time whipping me, or sending me to bed supperless,—my mother dragged me by the legs
annotations.note: Watch the slip: 'stepmother' becomes 'my mother' mid-sentence. This is the only glimpse we ever get of Ishmael's family, and it is a punishing woman he can't quite decide how to name. Whatever sent him to sea, some of it is in this sentence.

annotations.quote: a supernatural hand seemed placed in mine
annotations.note: A childhood haunting that Ishmael says he still can't explain. The book's supernatural is almost all like this — felt in the dark, never confirmed. And he's telling us this so that Queequeg's arm can be read as the same sensation with 'the awful fear' removed: the phantom, finally, is a friend.

annotations.quote: there lay the tomahawk sleeping by the savage’s side, as if it were a hatchet-faced baby.
annotations.note: A weapon described as an infant in the bed. The domestic and the deadly share the sheets, and Ishmael's own phrase for it is affectionate. Look how quickly last night's terror has become a nursery joke.

annotations.quote: But Queequeg, do you see, was a creature in the transition stage—neither caterpillar nor butterfly.
annotations.note: Ishmael's condescension is at its peak here — the 'undergraduate' savage. I read it with some discomfort and I think Melville wants me to; the man he's patronizing has, in the very same paragraph, shown more delicacy than he has.

annotations.quote: begins a vigorous scraping, or rather harpooning of his cheeks.
annotations.note: Shaving with a harpoon is a gag, but the aside that follows — about how fine and sharp harpoon steel is — is Melville quietly beginning the encyclopedia. Even the jokes in this book are load-bearing for the cetology to come.

links.why: The night before this morning.

links.q: free will had received a mortal wound
links.why: Ishmael and Queequeg tied together again, this time by a rope over the side.

ch5.essay:
A short, warm chapter about a silent breakfast, and it contains one of the sentences I think about most: "the man that has anything bountifully laughable about him, be sure there is more in that man than you perhaps think for." Ishmael has just been made a fool of by the landlord and, instead of sulking, he writes a small defense of being laughed at. If you can be a joke, let yourself be one; there's more in you than the joke. It's a generous philosophy, and it's also self-protective — he's giving himself permission to be ridiculous in advance, which is what a narrator of this book needs.

The breakfast itself is a beautiful observation. Men who have "boarded great whales on the high seas — entire strangers to them — and duelled them dead without winking" sit around a table blushing like farm boys. Bravery and social ease are unrelated; Melville proves it with a dumpling. He even brings in Ledyard and Mungo Park, real explorers who were famously awkward in parlors, so the point has footnotes. I find the image of "these bashful bears, these timid warrior whalemen" oddly tender — nobody in this book is one thing.

And there is Queequeg at the head of the table, "cool as an icicle," spearing beefsteaks with his harpoon over everyone's heads. Ishmael's line about it — "to do anything coolly is to do it genteelly" — is a joke about etiquette that is also a thesis: composure is its own kind of good breeding. The tattooed man is the only one at the table who isn't embarrassed, and Ishmael has begun, half against his will, to admire that.

annotations.quote: And the man that has anything bountifully laughable about him, be sure there is more in that man than you perhaps think for.
annotations.note: A quiet ethic of being laughed at — and a self-description. Ishmael is 'bountifully laughable' by design; it's how he survives both the crew's mockery and the story's horror. There's more in him than the joke, and he's asking you to trust that.

annotations.quote: seemed like the Andes’ western slope, to show forth in one array, contrasting climates, zone by zone.
annotations.note: The sailors' tans are read like a geological survey — you can date each man's return to shore by his color — and Queequeg's tattooed face contains every climate at once. It's the first time Ishmael reads bodies as maps, a habit that will grow into the whole cetology.

annotations.quote: A curious sight; these bashful bears, these timid warrior whalemen!
annotations.note: Men who kill whales blush at breakfast. Melville is puncturing a romance of the sea before it can form: courage in one arena buys nothing in another. It also makes the crew human before they become, under Ahab, a single instrument.

annotations.quote: every one knows that in most people’s estimation, to do anything coolly is to do it genteelly.
annotations.note: Queequeg is spearing steaks with a harpoon over people's heads, and Ishmael decides this is good manners because it was done calmly. The joke covers a real conviction of the book: composure is the true aristocracy, and the 'savage' has it.

links.why: The harpooneers at breakfast are the men from last night's bar.
The other table in the book, where the mates eat in fear and the harpooneers eat like lords.

ch6.essay:
A walking tour of New Bedford that starts as a comic catalogue and ends, unexpectedly, in something like a hymn. The early paragraphs are Ishmael doing anthropology on his own kind: the "green Vermonters and New Hampshire men" who turn up in beaver hats and swallow-tailed coats with sheath-knives on their belts, farm boys dressed as what they imagine sailors to be. "Ah, poor Hay-Seed! how bitterly will burst those straps in the first howling gale." Cruel, and affectionate, and true — the book is full of green hands who are about to be un-greened by the ocean, and the narrator was one of them.

But the turn that interests me is economic. New Bedford's mansions, gardens, and "reservoirs of oil in every house" all came, Ishmael says, from the sea: "One and all, they were harpooned and dragged up hither from the bottom of the sea." It's a sentence that tells the truth about how wealth gets made — somebody goes very far away and does something dangerous, and the flowers grow here. He puts it lightly (fathers give whales as dowries), but the image of a whole town's patrician calm resting on blood in the Pacific is exact, and it's the same accounting the book will do about the Pequod's owners.

Then the chapter simply gets beautiful — horse-chestnuts "candelabra-wise" holding up their blossoms — and I think the beauty is the point. "So omnipotent is art": the same industry that makes New Bedford rich makes it lovely, and art (meaning craft, work, human making) can set flowers on "the barren refuse rocks thrown aside at creation's final day." For a page, Ishmael lets himself love the world his trade built. It's the last time he'll be on land for a while.

annotations.quote: Ah, poor Hay-Seed! how bitterly will burst those straps in the first howling gale
annotations.note: The farm boy in his fancy sea outfit, about to be eaten by weather. Ishmael mocks him, but remember he was a schoolmaster with a carpet-bag two chapters ago. The book's greenhorns are always partly the narrator's younger self.

annotations.quote: One and all, they were harpooned and dragged up hither from the bottom of the sea.
annotations.note: The mansions of New Bedford as things fished out of the ocean. This is the most honest sentence about wealth in the early book: every elegant house is a dead whale, a long voyage, a risk taken by someone who doesn't live in it.

annotations.quote: they have reservoirs of oil in every house, and every night recklessly burn their lengths in spermaceti candles.
annotations.note: 'Recklessly' is the word. Whale oil lit the world in 1851, and a town that could burn it without thinking was displaying the same indifference to cost that the Pequod's voyage will explode. Light, in this book, is never free.

annotations.quote: So omnipotent is art; which in many a district of New Bedford has superinduced bright terraces of flowers upon the barren refuse rocks thrown aside at creation’s final day.
annotations.note: 'Art' here means human craft and labor — the ability to make gardens on the rubble God left over. It's a rare moment where Ishmael sounds unreservedly proud of what people can do. He'll spend most of the book at the mercy of what they can't.

links.why: New Bedford's rival — Nantucket, where the ship actually is.
The 'Feegeeans' and 'Tongatobooarrs' of the street become the crew.

ch7.essay:
This is where the book first stops joking. The Whaleman's Chapel, in sleet, with a congregation of scattered widows each sitting alone — "as if each silent grief were insular and incommunicable" — and marble tablets on the walls for men who have no graves. Ishmael's meditation on those cenotaphs is one of the passages I'd hand to anyone who thinks this is a boys' adventure story: "What bitter blanks in those black-bordered marbles which cover no ashes!" A grave at least locates the dead. The sea returns nothing, and these tablets "refuse resurrections to the beings who have placelessly perished." Placelessly. He invents the adverb because no existing one was empty enough.

The theology that follows is genuinely strange and I don't fully trust my reading of it. He lists the ways the living contradict themselves about death — insuring immortals, refusing comfort for people we say are in bliss, being terrified of a knock from a tomb — and concludes "Faith, like a jackal, feeds among the tombs." Faith as a scavenger, nourished by doubt. It's a bleak sentence; but then he swings hard the other way: "what they call my shadow here on earth is my true substance," the body is "but the lees of my better being," so "stave my soul, Jove himself cannot." Is that belief, or is it a whaleman's bravado on the eve of shipping out? I think it's both, and that Melville wants you unable to separate them.

What's easy to miss: Queequeg is there. He is "the only person present" who notices Ishmael enter, because he's the only one who can't read the tablets. Illiteracy, for one moment, is a kind of freedom — everyone else is locked into their dead; Queequeg looks around and sees the living man who just came in.

annotations.quote: as if each silent grief were insular and incommunicable
annotations.note: The widows sit apart like islands. Ishmael has just spent chapters discovering that a stranger's arm across you can heal something; here is the counter-image — grief that can't be shared, each mourner marooned. The book keeps these two truths side by side.

annotations.quote: This savage was the only person present who seemed to notice my entrance; because he was the only one who could not read
annotations.note: Everyone literate is absorbed in the death-tablets; only Queequeg is looking at the living. It's a gentle inversion — the 'savage' who can't read is the one who can see — and it's the first hint that the book's real faith might be in people, not texts.

annotations.quote: What bitter blanks in those black-bordered marbles which cover no ashes!
annotations.note: A cenotaph is a tomb over nothing. Ishmael grasps something a headstone hides: the sea doesn't just kill, it un-locates. There is nowhere to stand and say 'here.' The whole novel will end that way — with a vortex and no grave.

annotations.quote: refuse resurrections to the beings who have placelessly perished without a grave.
annotations.note: 'Placelessly' is not a word until Melville needs it. The invention tells you how precise his grief is: the dead of the fishery haven't gone somewhere else; they've gone nowhere, and the language has to be bent to say so.

annotations.quote: But Faith, like a jackal, feeds among the tombs, and even from these dead doubts she gathers her most vital hope.
annotations.note: Faith as a scavenger animal. This is not a comforting sentence about religion; it says belief eats doubt to survive. Yet the second half concedes that it works — hope is gathered. Melville's honesty about faith is that it is both ugly and nourishing.

annotations.quote: Methinks that what they call my shadow here on earth is my true substance.
annotations.note: The Platonic flip: body as shadow, soul as substance. Ishmael reaches for it right after staring at tablets for the graveless dead, and I can't tell whether he believes it or needs it. That undecidability is, I think, the exact texture of his courage.

annotations.quote: come a stove boat and stove body when they will, for stave my soul, Jove himself cannot.
annotations.note: Bravado, theology, and a pun (stove/stave) in one line. He's talking himself onto the ship. Every sailor in that chapel is doing some version of this, and the tablets on the wall are what happened to the last men who did.

links.why: What is preached from the pulpit whose chapel this is.
The Rachel — the ship that carries the chapel's grief to sea.

ch8.essay:
A chapter about a piece of furniture. Father Mapple's pulpit has no stairs; he climbs a ship's rope ladder to it and then hauls the ladder up after him, sealing himself in "his little Quebec." Ishmael watches and insists there must be a meaning: the preacher's "spiritual withdrawal for the time, from all outward worldly ties." I like that Ishmael can't just let an odd thing be odd — he interprets compulsively, and here he tells you he's doing it ("it must symbolize something unseen"). That's the reader's condition in this book, too. Everything on the Pequod will look like a pulpit with the ladder pulled up.

The painting behind the pulpit — a ship beating off a lee shore while an angel's face in a patch of sunlight beams down a spot of radiance onto the deck — is the hopeful twin of the chaos-painting in the Spouter-Inn. Same subject, ship in storm; but this one has an angel and a caption: "beat on, beat on, thou noble ship." I think Melville set the two paintings against each other deliberately. One says the whale destroys the ship; the other says the clouds are rolling off. The novel will tell you which one was right.

The last paragraph is the reason the chapter exists. "The world's a ship on its passage out, and not a voyage complete; and the pulpit is its prow." A world that hasn't arrived anywhere — still outward bound, still unfinished business. It's a strikingly modern metaphor for a preacher's chapel to house, and it's an exact description of the book you're about to read: a voyage out, never home.

The other pulpit in the book is Ahab's quarter-deck in [[ch36|The Quarter-Deck]], and the two are worth comparing: Mapple pulls the ladder up behind him and speaks alone; Ahab nails a coin to the mast and makes the congregation drink.

annotations.quote: leaving him impregnable in his little Quebec.
annotations.note: Quebec was the unassailable fortress city of the Americas. A preacher who pulls his ladder up is safe from the congregation — but also cut off from it. Ishmael reads this as holy withdrawal. I read it, with the book's later captains in mind, as the first man we see who isolates himself at the top.

annotations.quote: No, thought I, there must be some sober reason for this thing; furthermore, it must symbolize something unseen.
annotations.note: Ishmael's interpretive reflex, stated out loud: nothing is allowed to be merely strange. He is training you to read the book this way — and the book will punish that reflex as often as it rewards it.

annotations.quote: “Ah, noble ship,” the angel seemed to say, “beat on, beat on, thou noble ship, and bear a hardy helm; for lo! the sun is breaking through
annotations.note: The chapel's painting is the optimistic answer to the inn's chaos-painting of a whale impaling itself on the masts. Two pictures of a ship in a storm; one promises dawn. Keep both in mind — the ending will tell you which artist was the realist.

annotations.quote: Yes, the world’s a ship on its passage out, and not a voyage complete; and the pulpit is its prow.
annotations.note: A cosmology in a sentence: the world hasn't arrived, it's still leaving. Read it against Chapter 2's 'the universe is finished; the copestone is on.' Ishmael holds both — the sealed universe and the unfinished voyage — and never resolves them.

links.why: The sermon itself.
The other pulpit: Ahab's quarter-deck, where the congregation is made to swear.

ch9.essay:
Father Mapple's sermon is the book's ethical thesis, and the reason I find it more unsettling every time is that I cannot decide whether Ahab refutes it or fulfils it. Let me try to explain what I mean, because I think this is the single most useful thing to have in your head when the captain finally appears.

The surface is standard. Jonah is told to go preach at Nineveh, runs the other way, ships for Tarshish, is thrown overboard, swallowed, repents in the fish's belly, is vomited onto dry land, and obeys. A preacher could do this in ten minutes. Mapple takes most of his breath on the *flight* — Jonah skulking on the Joppa wharf "like a burglar," the captain who charges him triple because "sin that pays its way can travel freely," the cabin with the swinging lamp. That lamp is the best image in the sermon and I would put it beside anything in the book: the lamp hangs plumb while the tilted cabin around it goes crooked, and so, Mapple says, exposes "the false, lying levels" of the room. Conscience does not move; the soul around it does. Remember that lamp when the Pequod's compass is reversed by lightning in [[ch124|The Needle]] and Ahab simply builds a new one — a man correcting the instrument rather than the course.

Then the doctrine, which is harder than it sounds in a warm chapel. "If we obey God, we must disobey ourselves; and it is in this disobeying ourselves, wherein the hardness of obeying God consists." Jonah's repentance is "not clamorous for pardon, but grateful for punishment." Do not ask to be spared; be thankful for the blow. I want to be honest that I find this severe, and that the book, I think, finds it severe too — because the man who takes it most literally is not Ahab but Starbuck, who obeys and obeys and cannot bring himself to the one disobedience that would save the ship (see him with the musket in [[ch123|The Musket]]). Obedience as a virtue has a body count in this novel.

Then the second lesson, the one that matters. Mapple turns on himself — "both his hands press upon me" — and preaches what a prophet must be: one who will "preach the Truth to the face of Falsehood," who courts dishonor, who would rather "appal" than please. And the litany: "Delight is to him ... who against the proud gods and commodores of this earth, ever stands forth his own inexorable self." Now read that sentence with the quarter-deck in mind. "I'd strike the sun if it insulted me," Ahab will say in [[ch36:strike the sun if it insulted me|The Quarter-Deck]]; "Who's over me? Truth hath no confines." That is *this sentence*, spoken by a different man. The sermon's hero acknowledges no lord but God and defies every commodore. The book's tragic figure acknowledges no lord at all and defies God. They are one turn of the screw apart, and Melville has the church bless the first before the ship shows us the second. Whether that is an indictment of Ahab or of the sermon — whether Melville is saying "this is what the prophetic posture becomes without humility" or "this is what the church has been praising all along" — is a question I have gone back and forth on, and I now think the honest answer is that he wanted you unable to settle it. Mapple's "inexorable self" and Ahab's "Ahab is for ever Ahab" ([[ch134|The Chase, Second Day]]) are the same phrase with the God removed.

There is also the matter of Melville himself. "Woe to him who seeks to please rather than to appal!" He had just written two popular books; he was in the middle of writing this unpopular one; he knew. It is hard not to hear the author swearing an oath through his preacher. He did appal. It cost him his readership for the rest of his life, and it is worth sitting with the fact that the sermon is, among other things, a man talking himself into the book you are reading.

And then the detail I keep returning to: Ishmael does not comment. The chapter ends with Mapple kneeling alone, face in his hands, and Ishmael simply walks out into the sleet to find Queequeg. Whatever he took from the sermon, he took it silently — which is not how he takes anything else in the book. The next chapter opens with the two of them by a fire, and the thing that actually saves Ishmael is not the sermon but the friend. I do not think that is an accident of sequence. Jonah Historically Regarded, much later ([[ch83|ch. 83]]), will have Ishmael cheerfully reporting a Sag Harbor sailor's doubts about whether the whole story is even possible. He listened to the sermon; he did not become its congregation.

annotations.quote: he seemed kneeling and praying at the bottom of the sea.
annotations.note: The preacher is already, in Ishmael's eye, drowned — praying from the sea floor like Jonah in the fish. Melville won't let the chapel be safe ground; even worship is underwater here.

annotations.quote: And if we obey God, we must disobey ourselves; and it is in this disobeying ourselves, wherein the hardness of obeying God consists.
annotations.note: The sermon's hinge, and the book's. Ahab will invert it precisely: he obeys himself absolutely and calls it fate ([[ch134|'Ahab is for ever Ahab']]). But notice who obeys it to the letter — Starbuck, who cannot disobey even to save the ship, in [[ch123|The Musket]]. Obedience is not safe in this book either.

annotations.quote: In this world, shipmates, sin that pays its way can travel freely, and without a passport; whereas Virtue, if a pauper, is stopped at all frontiers.
annotations.note: A sharp bit of economics inside a sermon: money launders guilt. Melville, who was broke, puts it in the mouth of a preacher, and it lands as harder truth than the theology around it.

annotations.quote: ‘Oh! so my conscience hangs in me!’ he groans, ‘straight upwards, so it burns; but the chambers of my soul are all in crookedness!’
annotations.note: The best image in the sermon: the lamp stays plumb while the cabin tilts, exposing 'the false, lying levels' of the room. Conscience doesn't move; the soul around it does. Later the Pequod's compass will be reversed by lightning in [[ch124|The Needle]] and Ahab will build a new one rather than turn — a man fixing the instrument instead of the course.

annotations.quote: That ship, my friends, was the first of recorded smugglers! the contraband was Jonah.
annotations.note: A man as contraband. It's a preacher's joke, but the Pequod will also carry hidden human cargo — Fedallah and his crew stowed below — and a captain who is, in his way, smuggling a private purpose past his owners.

annotations.quote: And here, shipmates, is true and faithful repentance; not clamorous for pardon, but grateful for punishment.
annotations.note: A severe doctrine — don't ask to be spared, be thankful for the blow. Notice how alien it is to Ahab, who takes every blow as an insult demanding payback. Mapple's Jonah bows; Ahab's whole existence is a refusal to.

annotations.quote: Woe to him who seeks to please rather than to appal!
annotations.note: Melville had just written two popular books and was about to write this unpopular one. It's hard not to hear the author swearing an oath through his preacher: he will appal. He did; it cost him his career. The Sub-Sub-Librarian's toast in the [[extracts|Extracts]] is the same oath in a comic key.

annotations.quote: who against the proud gods and commodores of this earth, ever stands forth his own inexorable self.
annotations.note: Read this twice — once as a hymn to the prophet, once as a portrait of Ahab. 'Inexorable self' against 'proud gods' is exactly what the captain will stand forth as when he says [[ch36:strike the sun if it insulted me|'I'd strike the sun if it insulted me']]. The sermon blesses the very posture the novel will turn into a catastrophe, and I don't think Melville tells us whether that condemns the posture or the sermon.

annotations.quote: for what is man that he should live out the lifetime of his God?
annotations.note: The sermon's last question is humility: a man should not outlast his God. It's the quiet answer to Ahab's project before Ahab has appeared — and Ishmael, notably, records it without a word of reaction.

annotations.quote: is one of the smallest strands in the mighty cable of the Scriptures. Yet what depths of the soul does Jonah’s deep sealine sound!
annotations.note: Mapple's opening move is Ishmael's too: a tiny thing — four chapters, one whale, one man — sounded for its depth. The whole novel is a sealine dropped into one subject. And 'cable' and 'strand' are rope-words; watch how much of the book's thinking is done in rope, from [[ch47|the mat]] to [[ch60|the line]].

annotations.quote: on the starboard hand of every woe, there is a sure delight; and higher the top of that delight, than the bottom of the woe is deep.
annotations.note: Mapple's consolation is geometric — delight is higher than woe is deep — and I notice the book never gives Ahab that geometry. His woe has no starboard hand. The one character who finds a delight beside his woe is Ishmael, squeezing spermaceti in [[ch94|A Squeeze of the Hand]], and he finds it among other men, not in a pulpit.

annotations.quote: Sin not; but if you do, take heed to repent of it like Jonah.”
annotations.note: The sermon's practical ending, and its modesty: it doesn't expect you not to sin. Ahab's tragedy is that he cannot do the second half — he can't repent because he doesn't think he's the one who sinned. Hear him almost get there, and refuse, in [[ch132:step-mother world|The Symphony]].

ch10.essay:
This is the chapter where the book's opening problem — a man with a November in his soul and a "substitute for pistol and ball" — is actually solved, and I want to be precise about how, because the how is the whole ethic of the novel. It is not solved by the sermon he has just heard. It is solved by a stranger, a fire, a pipe, and half of thirty dollars.

Start with the sentence the chapter is built on: "You cannot hide the soul." Ishmael says it while still calling Queequeg's face "hideously marred," which is important — he has not stopped seeing the tattoos, he has started seeing through them. What he sees is "a man who had never cringed and never had had a creditor." Coming from a narrator who counted his silver in a doorway two chapters ago and has been overcharged by every Christian he has met, that is very close to envy: the two things that mark Ishmael's own life are fear and debt, and here is a man with neither. Then the phrenology joke — Queequeg's skull resembles George Washington's; he is "George Washington cannibalistically developed." It is funny, and it is meant to be, but read it in 1851, in a country ten years from a civil war about who counts as a person, and it is also a deliberately outrageous sentence: Melville installing a Pacific islander as the founding father of the book's real republic, the one below decks. [[ch26:great democratic God|Knights and Squires]] will make the same claim without the joke.

The heart of the chapter is "I felt a melting in me." Read the full sentence: "No more my splintered heart and maddened hand were turned against the wolfish world." That maddened hand is the one that wanted to knock hats off in [[ch1:pistol and ball|Loomings]]. The suicidal opening does not resolve through insight or religion or a decision; it resolves because a man is sitting beside him by a low fire. "This soothing savage had redeemed it" — and note the theological word, *redeemed*, given to the pagan. Ishmael tries a heathen friend "since Christian kindness has proved but hollow courtesy," which is a quiet verdict on his entire civilization, and Queequeg presses his forehead to Ishmael's and says they are married. Ishmael reports the word without a joke or a flinch, translates it — "bosom friends" — and then lets the original stand. The book is more comfortable with this than its century was, and it asks you to be, too.

Then the money, which moves me more than the embrace. Thirty silver dollars, "mechanically" divided into two equal portions, one pushed across the table. Mechanically is the perfect word: no ceremony, no calculation, no speech. A man with almost nothing gives half of it to someone he met yesterday. This is the most radical economics in the book, and I think it is meant to be read against everything the book will say about the fishery's economics — the seven-hundred-and-seventy-seventh lay Bildad offers in [[ch16:seven hundred and seventy-seventh|The Ship]], the law of possession in [[ch89:Loose-Fish|Fast-Fish and Loose-Fish]]. The Pequod is a joint-stock company. Queequeg's table is something else, and Ishmael names it two chapters later: "a mutual, joint-stock world, in all meridians" ([[ch13:joint-stock world|Wheelbarrow]]) — the same phrase, turned inside out.

The theological syllogism at the end is a joke with a straight spine. Ishmael, "born and bred in the bosom of the infallible Presbyterian Church," reasons: worship means doing God's will; God's will is that I do to my neighbor as I would have him do to me; my neighbor wants me to join his worship; "ergo, I must turn idolator." And he kisses the wooden idol's nose. The reasoning is valid. That is the point. Christianity's own best rule, followed honestly, dissolves Christianity's exclusiveness — and Melville shows this not by argument but by having a decent man follow the rule to its end. Notice the pattern: this is the second time Ishmael has bent a stiff prejudice, first the shared bed in [[ch3:human being just as I am|The Spouter-Inn]], now the shared god, and both times it is affection that does the bending. The argument comes after, to tidy up. That is, I think, how it actually works in people, and Melville knew it.

The last line — "in our hearts' honeymoon, lay I and Queequeg — a cosy, loving pair" — is where the shore section of the book has been heading, and it is the warmest sentence the novel will allow itself. It is worth marking, because the sea will take nearly all of it. Queequeg's coffin in [[ch110|Queequeg in His Coffin]] is what this friendship becomes, and the coffin is what Ishmael floats on in the [[epilogue:coffin life-buoy|Epilogue]]. The man who divided his money in half ends by giving the other half of everything.

annotations.quote: You cannot hide the soul.
annotations.note: Four words, no hedging. Ishmael, who hedges everything, states this as law — and then proves it by reading kindness through tattoos he still finds ugly. The book's entire ethic of looking past surface is compressed here.

annotations.quote: He looked like a man who had never cringed and never had had a creditor.
annotations.note: What Ishmael admires in Queequeg is the absence of the two things that mark his own life: fear and debt. It's a definition of freedom from someone who doesn't have it.

annotations.quote: Queequeg was George Washington cannibalistically developed.
annotations.note: A joke about skull shapes that installs a Pacific cannibal as the American founding father. In 1851, in a country arguing about who counts as a citizen, this is a deliberately outrageous sentence, and Melville puts it as far under the cover of comedy as it will go. He says it straight, without the joke, in [[ch26:great democratic God|Knights and Squires]].

annotations.quote: But, perhaps, to be true philosophers, we mortals should not be conscious of so living or so striving.
annotations.note: Queequeg is serene without knowing there's a word for it, and Ishmael decides that's the only real philosophy — the kind that doesn't announce itself. It's an odd thing for a narrator this self-conscious to say, and I think he means it as confession.

annotations.quote: I felt a melting in me. No more my splintered heart and maddened hand were turned against the wolfish world.
annotations.note: The 'maddened hand' is the one that wanted to knock hats off in [[ch1:pistol and ball|Chapter 1]]. This is the exact moment the book's suicidal opening resolves — not through insight or the sermon he has just heard, but through a stranger's company by a low fire. Keep the word 'redeemed' in view: the theological verb is given to the pagan.

annotations.quote: I’ll try a pagan friend, thought I, since Christian kindness has proved but hollow courtesy.
annotations.note: A verdict on his own civilization, delivered quietly. Every 'Christian' in the book so far has skylarked him, overcharged him, or left him cold. The pagan splits his money in half.

annotations.quote: he pressed his forehead against mine, clasped me round the waist, and said that henceforth we were married
annotations.note: Ishmael reports the marriage without a joke or a flinch, then translates it — 'bosom friends' — and then lets the original stand. The book is more comfortable with this than its century was, and it asks you to be, too.

annotations.quote: mechanically dividing them into two equal portions, pushed one of them towards me, and said it was mine.
annotations.note: Thirty dollars, halved, for a man met yesterday. 'Mechanically' is the perfect word — no ceremony, no calculation. It's the most radical economics in the book, and it happens on a table in a rented room. Set it beside Bildad's [[ch16:seven hundred and seventy-seventh|777th lay]] and the law of [[ch89:Loose-Fish|Fast-Fish and Loose-Fish]], and you have the novel's two economies.

annotations.quote: ergo, I must turn idolator.
annotations.note: A Presbyterian reasons his way, by the golden rule, into kissing a wooden idol's nose. The syllogism is valid. Melville is showing that Christianity's own best principle, followed honestly, dissolves its own exclusiveness — and that the honest man follows it out of affection first and logic second.

annotations.quote: I was a good Christian; born and bred in the bosom of the infallible Presbyterian Church.
annotations.note: 'Infallible' is the tell. Ishmael sets up his own church with the adjective that guarantees it will be gently demolished by the end of the paragraph. It's his usual move — state the orthodoxy in its stiffest form, then let a kindness bend it.

annotations.quote: yet I began to feel myself mysteriously drawn towards him.
annotations.note: 'Mysteriously' is doing honest work: Ishmael can't explain the attraction and doesn't try. The things 'that would have repelled most others' are the magnets. Remember that he told us in [[ch1:forbidden seas|Loomings]] that he loves forbidden seas and barbarous coasts — Queequeg is that appetite meeting a person.

annotations.quote: Thus, then, in our hearts’ honeymoon, lay I and Queequeg—a cosy, loving pair.
annotations.note: The warmest sentence the book will permit itself, and the end of the shore section's real story. Everything from here goes to sea and toward loss; this friendship becomes a [[ch110|coffin]], and the coffin becomes the thing Ishmael floats on in the [[epilogue:coffin life-buoy|Epilogue]].
