ch11.essay:
A tiny chapter, mostly two men sitting up in a cold bed with their knees drawn up, and it contains one of the ideas I most associate with the whole book: "there is no quality in this world that is not what it is merely by contrast. Nothing exists in itself." You can only feel warm if some part of you is cold. He derives a rule of interior design from this (no fires in bedrooms) but the principle is far bigger than blankets. It's a theory of knowledge — you know a thing by its edge, by where it meets its opposite — and it will underwrite the terror of the white whale, which is horrible precisely because whiteness is *absence* of contrast, everything and nothing at once.

The image that follows is perfect: "like the one warm spark in the heart of an arctic crystal." That's the human condition as Ishmael sees it — a spark, a crystal of cold all around, and the snugness is real only because the cold is real. Then a second odd claim: "no man can ever feel his own identity aright except his eyes be closed; as if darkness were indeed the proper element of our essences." Ishmael keeps his eyes shut in bed to concentrate the feeling of being himself. It's the kind of thing a person says once, to a friend, at midnight, and Melville has caught it exactly.

And there's the pipe. The night before, Ishmael refused to let Queequeg smoke in bed ("I ain't insured"). Now: "see how elastic our stiff prejudices grow when love once comes to bend them." A rule that was a rule yesterday. This is how the book models change — not by argument, but by affection making the argument unnecessary.

annotations.quote: for there is no quality in this world that is not what it is merely by contrast. Nothing exists in itself.
annotations.note: A whole epistemology in a cold bed. Warmth needs a cold nose to be felt; every quality is known by its edge. Hold onto this when you reach the chapter on whiteness — the terror there is a color that abolishes contrast.

annotations.quote: Then there you lie like the one warm spark in the heart of an arctic crystal.
annotations.note: The most beautiful image of coziness I know, and it's built entirely out of surrounding cold. Ishmael's happiness is always like this: a small lit thing that knows exactly how much dark is around it.

annotations.quote: no man can ever feel his own identity aright except his eyes be closed; as if darkness were indeed the proper element of our essences
annotations.note: Selfhood is best felt in the dark. It's a strange, private claim that Melville presents without argument, as though everyone secretly knows it. I think of it every time the book's characters stare into black water and see themselves.

annotations.quote: yet see how elastic our stiff prejudices grow when love once comes to bend them.
annotations.note: Yesterday, no smoking in bed; today, delight in it. Ishmael names the mechanism plainly: prejudice doesn't get refuted, it gets bent by fondness. It's the gentlest account of moral change in the book — and the one Ahab's crew will fail to apply to Ahab.

links.why: How they came to be sharing a bed so easily.
Queequeg's story, told in this same bed.

ch12.essay:
"It is not down in any map; true places never are." I think that's one of the finest sentences in the book, and it opens a chapter that's nominally a biography. Rokovoko is invented (Melville changed the spelling from an earlier draft); the point is that Queequeg's origin can't be located by Christendom's instruments, and that this makes it more real, not less. The line also quietly reframes the whole voyage: the Pequod is going somewhere unmapped, and the things that matter there won't be on charts either.

The story itself is a reversal of the missionary narrative. A Polynesian prince wants to see Christendom — paddles out alone, capsizes his own canoe so there's no going back, grabs a ring-bolt and swears "not to let it go, though hacked in pieces" — because he hopes to learn from Christians "the arts whereby to make his people still happier than they were; and more than that, still better." And what he learns, in Sag Harbor and Nantucket, is that Christians are "both miserable and wicked; infinitely more so, than all his father's heathens." "It's a wicked world in all meridians; I'll die a pagan." Melville had lived among Marquesan islanders and watched missionaries at work; this is his verdict, given to the one character who earned the right to make it.

The detail I find saddest is that Queequeg won't go home to be crowned because he feels Christianity has "unfitted him" for the pure throne of his fathers — he's waiting "until he felt himself baptized again." He's been contaminated by us and knows it. The harpoon "was in lieu of a sceptre now." A king in exile, working for wages, choosing to share Ishmael's "every hap." Ishmael says he assented "joyously." After the chapel and the sermon, this is the book's actual sacrament: two men agreeing to be in the same boat.

annotations.quote: It is not down in any map; true places never are.
annotations.note: Eleven words that unmoor the whole book from geography. Queequeg's home is real because it's uncharted — and by the same logic, the Pequod's destination will be a 'true place' no instrument can fix. The sentence is also, I think, Melville's quiet defense of fiction.

annotations.quote: with one backward dash of his foot capsized and sank his canoe
annotations.note: He destroys his own way home before he's been accepted aboard. It's the same gesture Ahab will make with the quadrant and the ship — burn the return — but Queequeg does it for curiosity and love of the world, not vengeance. Same courage, opposite direction.

annotations.quote: the practices of whalemen soon convinced him that even Christians could be both miserable and wicked; infinitely more so, than all his father’s heathens.
annotations.note: The missionary story run backward: the 'savage' comes to be improved and finds nothing to learn. Melville had watched missions in the Pacific firsthand and never forgave them. This is his report, delivered without raising his voice.

annotations.quote: Thought he, it’s a wicked world in all meridians; I’ll die a pagan.
annotations.note: The most level-headed theology in the book belongs to the man with the idol. It isn't despair — Queequeg remains the kindest person aboard — it's a decision to stop expecting any creed to fix people. He will indeed die a pagan, and better than anyone.

annotations.quote: he was fearful Christianity, or rather Christians, had unfitted him for ascending the pure and undefiled throne of thirty pagan Kings before him.
annotations.note: Notice the correction: 'Christianity, or rather Christians.' Queequeg doesn't blame the faith; he blames its practitioners, and feels contaminated by contact. A prince who can't go home because we've dirtied him — it's the book's quietest indictment.

annotations.quote: with both my hands in his, boldly dip into the Potluck of both worlds.
annotations.note: A potluck: whatever's in the pot, shared. Queequeg's proposal is total — same ship, same watch, same boat, same mess — and Ishmael's joyous assent is the closest thing to a wedding vow the novel contains. It's also, practically, what will save Ishmael's life.

links.why: Why Ishmael already trusts this man enough to hear his story.
The other time Queequeg tells his own story — from inside a coffin.

ch13.essay:
The wheelbarrow chapter is two comic stories and a rescue, and I think it's the moment Queequeg stops being a curiosity and becomes the moral center of the book. The stories first: Queequeg, not knowing what a wheelbarrow is for, lashes his chest to it and carries the whole thing on his shoulder up the wharf; and in return, a punctilious ship's captain at a wedding feast in Rokovoko washes his hands in the sacred punchbowl, thinking it a finger-glass. "Didn't our people laugh?" Both men made the same mistake — used a foreign object by their own rules. The difference is which one gets called a savage. Melville sets the two anecdotes side by side and lets the symmetry make the argument.

Then the passage down the Acushnet, and Ishmael's sudden bleak aside as he looks at ships refitting for new voyages: "one most perilous and long voyage ended, only begins a second; and a second ended, only begins a third, and so on, for ever and for aye. Such is the endlessness, yea, the intolerableness of all earthly effort." That's Ecclesiastes on a packet schooner. He shakes it off with sea air — "how I spurned that turnpike earth!" — but the intolerableness has been named.

And the rescue. A bumpkin mocks Queequeg; Queequeg tosses him in the air; the boom breaks loose and sweeps the bumpkin overboard; everyone freezes; Queequeg lassoes the boom, strips, dives into freezing water, and hauls up the man who mocked him. Then asks only for fresh water to wash off the brine. Ishmael's imagined caption — "It's a mutual, joint-stock world, in all meridians. We cannibals must help these Christians" — is the ethical thesis of the novel, put in a cannibal's mouth. And the line I can never get past: "From that hour I clove to Queequeg like a barnacle; yea, till poor Queequeg took his last long dive." The book tells you, in Chapter 13, that Queequeg dies. Ishmael can't help himself; his grief is ahead of his story.

The phrase 'a mutual, joint-stock world' is Ishmael's translation of the halved money in [[ch10:two equal portions|A Bosom Friend]] — and it will be quietly contradicted by the actual joint-stock company that owns the Pequod, whose first act in [[ch16:seven hundred and seventy-seventh|The Ship]] is to price him.

annotations.quote: he had a particular affection for his own harpoon, because it was of assured stuff, well tried in many a mortal combat, and deeply intimate with the hearts of whales.
annotations.note: A weapon described as intimate with the hearts of what it kills. It's the same tenderness the book will show for every tool of the trade — and it's the kind of reverent attention Ahab will bring to his own harpoon, forged and baptized in blood.

annotations.quote: “Now,” said Queequeg, “what you tink now?—Didn’t our people laugh?”
annotations.note: The captain washes his hands in the sacred punchbowl; Queequeg carried a wheelbarrow on his shoulder. Same error, mirror image. Melville has just demonstrated, in two anecdotes, that 'savage' means only 'unfamiliar with our particular bowl.'

annotations.quote: one most perilous and long voyage ended, only begins a second; and a second ended, only begins a third, and so on, for ever and for aye. Such is the endlessness, yea, the intolerableness of all earthly effort.
annotations.note: Ecclesiastes surfacing on a pleasant morning. Ishmael watches ships refit and sees Sisyphus. This despair is real and recurring in him, and it's worth noticing that what pulls him out isn't philosophy — it's a breeze and the sight of Queequeg drinking the same wind.

annotations.quote: and turned me to admire the magnanimity of the sea which will permit no records.
annotations.note: The land is 'dented with the marks of slavish heels'; the sea keeps no record. He's just come from a chapel full of tablets for men the sea erased, and here he calls that erasure magnanimous. Ishmael's love of the sea is inseparable from its indifference.

annotations.quote: as though a white man were anything more dignified than a whitewashed negro.
annotations.note: Dropped into a subordinate clause, in 1851, in a nation that counted Black people as three-fifths. The passengers stare at a white man and a Pacific islander being friends; Ishmael's contempt for their staring is quick and absolute.

annotations.quote: From that hour I clove to Queequeg like a barnacle; yea, till poor Queequeg took his last long dive.
annotations.note: The book tells you Queequeg will die, here, in Chapter 13, in an aside. Ishmael is narrating from after the wreck and can't keep his grief in sequence. Every warm scene with Queequeg from here on is shadowed by this half-sentence.

annotations.quote: “It’s a mutual, joint-stock world, in all meridians. We cannibals must help these Christians.”
annotations.note: Ishmael puts the novel's ethic into Queequeg's imagined thought: a joint-stock world, everyone a shareholder in everyone else. It's the exact opposite of Ahab's world, in which one man's grievance is allowed to spend everyone's life.

links.why: The halved money, which this chapter turns into a philosophy.
Tally: the cannibal saves the Christian who mocked him.

ch14.essay:
Nantucket, in this chapter, is barely land at all — "a mere hillock, and elbow of sand; all beach, without a background" — and Ishmael's tall tales about it (they import Canada thistles, they plant toadstools for shade, clams stick to the chairs) are among the gentlest comedy in the book. But the tall tales are a setup for something grander. The Nantucketer, born on a beach, went to sea by necessity and ended up owning "two thirds of this terraqueous globe." Other sailors have "a right of way" through the ocean; the Nantucketer "resides and riots" on it. The chapter is a myth of origin for a maritime empire, and it's told with real awe.

The Indian legend in the middle is the part I find haunting. An eagle carries off an infant; the parents paddle after it and find the island, and on it "an empty ivory casket, — the poor little Indian's skeleton." That's the founding of Nantucket: a search for a stolen child that ends in bones. Melville puts it there without comment and moves on to crabs and cod. But the whole chapter's triumphalism grows out of a grave, and the "ivory casket" foreshadows every ivory thing on the Pequod — Ahab's leg, the whale's jaw, the bone-white ship itself.

The last image redeems everything: the Nantucketer at nightfall, out of sight of land, furling his sails and lying down "while under his very pillow rush herds of walruses and whales." That's not conquest. That's a man asleep on the back of the thing he hunts, at peace with it. It's the last purely happy picture of the sea in the book, and I think Melville placed it on the doorstep of Nantucket, before Ahab, so we would know what was possible.

annotations.quote: a mere hillock, and elbow of sand; all beach, without a background.
annotations.note: 'Without a background' — an island with no depth behind it, all edge. It's a joke about geography, but it's also why these people went to sea: there was nothing to turn back toward. The Pequod will sail from a place that is already almost ocean.

annotations.quote: there they found an empty ivory casket,—the poor little Indian’s skeleton.
annotations.note: Nantucket is founded on a stolen child's bones. Melville tells it in one sentence and moves on, but this is the island's origin as he chooses to give it: a search that ends in ivory. Every ivory thing on the Pequod — Ahab's leg, the ship's bone trim — echoes this casket.

annotations.quote: That Himmalehan, salt-sea Mastodon, clothed with such portentousness of unconscious power, that his very panics are more to be dreaded than his most fearless and malicious assaults!
annotations.note: The whale's terror is 'unconscious power' — it doesn't mean to kill. The whole book will turn on whether that's true: Ishmael here says the whale's panics are worse than its malice; Ahab will insist the malice is real and personal. They're arguing about the same animal.

annotations.quote: For the sea is his; he owns it, as Emperors own empires; other seamen having but a right of way through it.
annotations.note: A sandbar's fishermen as emperors of two-thirds of the globe. Melville's pride in the American whaling fleet is unironic here, and it's worth feeling it fully, because the book is about what happens when that empire's finest ship is hijacked by one man's grief.

annotations.quote: so at nightfall, the Nantucketer, out of sight of land, furls his sails, and lays him to his rest, while under his very pillow rush herds of walruses and whales.
annotations.note: The last wholly peaceful image of the ocean in the book: a man asleep with whales rushing beneath his pillow, unafraid. This is the relationship to Leviathan that Ahab will make impossible. Melville shows it to you once, clearly, before taking it away.

links.why: The Pequod, and the Nantucketers who own her.
